title: Determiners and pronouns for reference
objectives: Use each and both in standard noun and pronoun patterns.
Use one, ones, former and latter with clear reference.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Determiners and pronouns help speakers refer to people and things without repeating a noun unnecessarily. A determiner normally appears before a noun: ‘both proposals’ or ‘each student’. A pronoun can stand in place of a noun phrase when the reference is clear: ‘Both are useful’ or ‘Each has a copy’.

Both, either and neither typically refer to two people or things. ‘Both options are available’ includes the two. ‘Either option is suitable’ means that one or the other is acceptable. ‘Neither option is suitable’ means that not one of the two is suitable. Context determines whether a sentence is discussing a choice, agreement or something else.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Before a noun, both can be followed by a plural noun: ‘both plans’. Both of can precede a determiner and plural noun or an object pronoun: ‘both of the plans’ and ‘both of them’. With a pronoun, use both of them, not ‘both them’ in standard English.

Each and every generally precede a singular countable noun and take a singular verb in this structure: ‘Each student has a copy’ and ‘Every student has a copy’. Each of can precede a plural noun phrase or object pronoun: ‘Each of the students has a copy’ and ‘Each of them has a copy’. A plural verb is also heard with some of these expressions in informal usage; the singular form is a reliable choice in formal writing.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: One and ones can replace a countable noun when the reference is clear: ‘I prefer the blue chair to the red one’ and ‘The larger boxes are cheaper than the smaller ones’. One normally represents a singular noun and ones a plural noun. They do not refer to people in every structure, and they are not used as simple replacements for uncountable nouns in all contexts.

The phrases the former and the latter refer respectively to the first and second of two previously mentioned things: ‘We considered the train and the bus; the former was faster’. These phrases can sound formal, and they are less useful if the reader must search back through a long passage. Repeating the noun may be clearer.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not assume that either and neither are interchangeable: ‘Either answer is acceptable’ permits one or the other; ‘Neither answer is acceptable’ rejects both. Do not follow each directly with a plural noun in the pattern ‘each student’: use ‘each student’ or ‘each of the students’.

A pronoun is useful only if its reference is clear. In ‘Maya called Ana after she arrived’, she could refer to Maya or Ana. Add a name when necessary. Repetition can improve clarity, and a different pronoun or a longer sentence may be preferable to an ambiguous shortcut.

summary: Both, either and neither have distinct meanings when referring to two things.
Use each with a singular noun, or each of with a plural noun phrase or object pronoun.
Use substitute words only when their reference is clear.
